Yes. 

The manipulation of time in the story is masterfully balanced to serve its emotional arc. The first half uses **compression of time** to summarize roughly fourteen years—four years of college and a decade of post-graduation drift—in just five paragraphs. This effectively establishes the mythos of "Q" as an effortlessly perfect person and explains the narrator's growing insecurity and resulting ten-year silence. 

In the second half, the pacing shifts dramatically to **stretching of time** (or real-time scene work), dedicating the rest of the story to a single, brief morning at a swimming pool. Slowing the narrative down to capture every word, pause, and facial expression during Q's awkward confrontation with Marianne allows the reader to experience the exact moment the narrator's decade-long illusion of Q shatters. The stark contrast between the compressed years of idealized memory and the stretched-out minutes of flawed reality makes the ending's emotional resolution feel earned and impactful.
